# Pet Nutrition & Bowl Calculator (by PawsOnMe)

> Free calculator for how much a dog (any breed or mix) or cat should eat each day, in calories and amount of food, and how high and how big its food bowl should be, from the pet's weight, food, elbow height and needs. Each number is labelled as a study result or a rule of thumb, with sources. Made by PawsOnMe, an Etsy shop of ceramic slow feeder bowls for cats and small to medium dogs: https://www.etsy.com/shop/PawsOnMePet

## Key answers
- Dog bowl height, from the floor to the top edge of the bowl: between elbow height and 5 to 7.5 cm (2 to 3 in) below it. Rule of thumb; no veterinary guideline sets a height.
- Large and giant breed dogs: height matters. In a cohort of 1,637 dogs, large breeds (23 to 45 kg) fed from a bowl raised 1 ft (30.5 cm) or less had 3.06 times the bloat (GDV) risk of floor-fed dogs, with no significant difference above 1 ft; giant breeds (over 45 kg) had 2.29 times the risk above 1 ft and no significant difference at 1 ft or less (Glickman et al., JAVMA 2000; Buckley, Veterinary Evidence 2017). So a raised bowl goes above 30.5 cm for a large breed and at 30.5 cm or lower for a giant breed. One study with 98 bloat cases; an internet survey found no clear effect of bowl height (Pipan et al., JAVMA 2012). Dogs with megaesophagus are fed from a raised position on purpose: front legs higher than back legs, then upright for at least 10 to 15 minutes after meals (Merck Veterinary Manual).
- Cats: most eat fine from the floor. Whisker-friendly dishes made no difference to eating in a 38-cat study, though 63% of owners said their cat preferred them (Slovak and Foster, JFMS 2021).
- Capacity: 1.5 times the meal volume, 2 times for a slow feeder. 1 US cup = 236.6 ml. Rule of thumb. Grams, ounces or cans are turned into volume with the food's weight per cup from foods.js: dry food = the maker's kcal per cup ÷ kcal per kg × 1,000; wet food 1.0 g per ml; fresh-cooked food 146.5 to 188 g a cup from the makers; freeze-dried 45 g a cup. A food that isn't listed takes the 10th percentile of its type, so the bowl errs big.
- Bringing food back up without retching (regurgitation) is not eating fast: it points to the food pipe, so a vet check, feeding from higher up and smaller meals more often (Merck), with no slow feeder. Being sick or licking the lips on an empty stomach for too long, often after overnight, is about meal timing: smaller meals through the day and a small late-evening meal (Ferguson et al., JAAHA 2016).
- How much to feed: resting energy = 70 x (weight in kg)^0.75 kcal a day; multiply by 1.6 for a spayed or neutered adult dog, 1.8 intact, 1.2 to 1.4 not very active, about 1.9 active (National Research Council), 2 for working detection dogs, and 1.2 for a spayed or neutered adult cat, about 1.6 for a very active or outdoor cat (FEDIAF 2025: active cats need about a third more than indoor or neutered cats), 2 to 3 for puppies and kittens (Pet Nutrition Alliance, Merck). Divide by kcal per cup on the bag (or by kcal per kg × 1,000 for grams); adjust to body condition.
- What to feed: a food labelled complete and balanced for the life stage; puppies that will be large dogs need a growth food that includes large size dogs.
- Slow feeders: in a study of 10 pet dogs, meals took significantly longer from a slow feeder, even after nine days of practice (Buckley and Lees 2016). Eating fast is a bloat (GDV) risk factor (Glickman et al. 1997, 2000), and VCA Animal Hospitals advises feeding large and giant dogs from the floor with a puzzle feeder or slow-down bowl. For cats, the AAFP consensus recommends frequent small meals from puzzle feeders (Sadek et al. 2018). Veterinary Partner (VIN) says small meals in feeders prevent gulping and may lessen vomiting, and suggests puzzle feeding bowls for dogs that swallow air by eating quickly (Yuschak 2024; Brooks 2026). No trial has tested bloat prevention itself.

## Second skill
- Low-fat and copper-restricted diet math for dogs (skills/dog-diet-fat-copper): RER = 70 x kg^0.75; fat line 24 g per 1000 kcal (Today's Veterinary Practice), AAFCO fat minimum 13.8 g per 1000 kcal; copper target for copper-associated hepatopathy < 1.2 mg per 1000 kcal (Today's Veterinary Practice 2025), AAFCO copper minimum 1.83 mg per 1000 kcal.
